name: Viral (Aseptic) Meningitis

pathogens.why: Enteroviruses cause the large majority of viral meningitis, typically with a more benign, self-limited course than bacterial meningitis. However, clinical differentiation from early bacterial meningitis is unreliable, which is why CSF analysis (lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, negative Gram stain/culture in viral meningitis) is essential rather than optional.

investigations.test: Lumbar puncture with CSF cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture
investigations.why: The decisive test distinguishing viral from bacterial meningitis and guiding the decision to continue or stop empiric antibacterial therapy.
Identifies the specific viral cause; HSV PCR specifically changes management since HSV meningitis/encephalitis is treated with acyclovir.
Performed alongside LP workup to support the broader diagnostic picture, particularly if bacterial meningitis cannot yet be excluded.

references: IDSA Bacterial Meningitis Guidelines (for exclusion criteria)
reason: Fever with neck stiffness and headache, WITHOUT altered consciousness, petechial rash, or seizure, raises the possibility of viral (aseptic) meningitis rather than bacterial meningitis. However, this distinction cannot be made on clinical grounds alone with confidence — lumbar puncture with CSF analysis is required, and empiric antibacterial therapy should generally still be started pending results unless bacterial meningitis can be confidently excluded by an experienced clinician, since the consequences of missing bacterial meningitis are severe.

clinicalPearls: Profound alterations in consciousness (stupor, coma, marked confusion), seizures, focal neurologic signs, or neuroimaging evidence of parenchymal involvement do NOT occur in viral meningitis; their presence points instead to encephalitis or another CNS process (p.1166).

Headache is almost invariably present, often frontal or retroorbital, with photophobia and pain on eye movement; nuchal rigidity is usually present but may be mild, appearing only near the limit of neck anteflexion (p.1166).

A specific viral cause is identified in 60-90% of cases using combined CSF PCR, culture, and serology; roughly two-thirds of culture-negative 'aseptic' meningitis cases have a viral etiology found by CSF PCR (p.1166).
Enteroviruses account for >85% of cases with an identified etiology and predominate in summer and fall, especially in children <15 years (p.1167-1168).

HSV-2 causes most adult uncomplicated HSV meningitis (HSV-1 causes ~90% of HSV encephalitis); ~20% of HSV meningitis patients develop recurrent attacks, and most recurrent/'aseptic' meningitis, including cases formerly called Mollaret's meningitis, is due to HSV (p.1168).
Many HSV meningitis patients give no history and show no active genital herpes lesions at presentation, so absence of genital lesions does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1168).
VZV is increasingly recognized as a cause of meningitis even WITHOUT rash, so absence of chickenpox or shingles does not exclude it (p.1168).

Cranial nerve palsies (most often V, VII, or VIII) are more common in HIV meningitis than in other viral meningitides; HIV seroconversion may be delayed, so seronegative suspected cases warrant repeat testing (p.1168).

Mumps meningitis is suggested by parotitis, orchitis, oophoritis, pancreatitis, or raised serum amylase/lipase, but their absence does not exclude it; a documented prior mumps infection (lifelong immunity) does exclude it (p.1168-1169).

Consider LCMV when aseptic meningitis occurs in late fall/winter with exposure to house mice or pet/laboratory rodents or their excreta, particularly when accompanied by leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or abnormal liver function tests (p.1169).
harrison.pathophysiology: Viral meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, most often caused by enteroviruses, with a self-limited course in immunocompetent hosts. Inflammation is largely confined to the meninges, producing meningeal irritation without the parenchymal brain involvement that characterizes encephalitis; preservation of higher cerebral function distinguishes meningitis from encephalitis. CSF oligoclonal IgG bands directed against viral proteins can occur, though they are nonspecific (Harrison 22e p.1166-1167).
additionalDifferentials: Arthropod-borne (arbovirus) meningitis, notably West Nile virus; consider when meningitis/encephalitis clusters occur in a restricted region in summer/early fall (p.1167-1168)
Epstein-Barr virus (may produce aseptic meningitis with or without infectious mononucleosis; atypical lymphocytes in CSF/blood are suggestive) (p.1168)
Cytomegalovirus (notably in immunocompromised hosts, where it may cause PMN pleocytosis with low glucose) (p.1167)
HSV-1 (less common cause of meningitis than HSV-2) (p.1167)
Human parechovirus (included on the FilmArray ME panel) (p.1167)
infectionMimics: Untreated or partially treated bacterial meningitis (a key pitfall when CSF shifts toward lymphocytic predominance) (p.1167)
Early fungal meningitis (lymphocytic pleocytosis common; hypoglycorrhachia may be absent early) (p.1167)
nonInfectiousMimics: Systemic lupus erythematosus and other rheumatologic diseases (p.1167)
additionalInvestigations: CSF reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) for enteroviruses: diagnostic procedure of choice, highest sensitivity if done within 48 h of symptom onset, falling rapidly after day 5 (p.1166, 1168)
FilmArray Meningitis/Encephalitis multiplex PCR panel covering HSV-1, HSV-2, enteroviruses, VZV, HHV-6, and human parechovirus (does NOT include CMV, WNV, LCMV, or EBV) (p.1166)
WNV-specific CSF IgM (more sensitive than CSF RT-PCR for WNV; RT-PCR ~70% sensitive, useful mainly in immunocompromised patients with poor antibody response) (p.1166, 1168)
Arboviral serology demonstrating CSF viral-specific IgM or seroconversion; repeat testing if early study is negative and suspicion is high (p.1168)
Throat washing and stool PCR/culture to support enteroviral (and Mycoplasma) diagnosis (stool/throat shedding may persist for weeks) (p.1166-1167)
Demonstration of intrathecal HSV-specific or VZV-specific antibody synthesis (less sensitive/specific than PCR; may take >1 week to become positive) (p.1168)
Routine bloods: complete blood count with differential, liver and renal function tests, ESR, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, glucose, creatine kinase, aldolase, amylase, and lipase (p.1167)
Neuroimaging (MRI preferred over CT) when there is altered consciousness, seizures, focal signs, atypical CSF profile, or immunocompromise (not mandatory in uncomplicated viral meningitis) (p.1167)
Serum procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL as a clue favoring bacterial over aseptic meningitis (p.1167)
redFlags: Depressed or markedly altered consciousness (stupor, coma, marked confusion) — suggests encephalitis or alternative diagnosis, not simple viral meningitis (p.1166)
Focal neurologic signs/symptoms or neuroimaging abnormalities indicating parenchymal brain involvement (p.1166)
CSF PMN pleocytosis without an established diagnosis — should prompt consideration of bacterial or parameningeal infection (p.1166-1167)

Lymphocytic pleocytosis WITH low CSF glucose (hypoglycorrhachia) — should raise suspicion of fungal, tuberculous, or Listeria meningoencephalitis, or noninfectious causes such as sarcoid or neoplastic meningitis (p.1167)
Atypical CSF profile or immunocompromising condition/treatment — warrants hospitalization and neuroimaging (p.1167)
harrison.prognosis: In adults the prognosis for full recovery from viral meningitis is excellent; treatment of almost all cases is primarily symptomatic. Rare adult patients have persisting headache, mild mental impairment, incoordination, or generalized asthenia for weeks to months. Outcome is less certain in infants and neonates (<1 year), in whom intellectual impairment, learning disabilities, hearing loss, and other lasting sequelae have been reported. Enteroviral meningitis outside the neonatal period is usually benign with recovery without sequelae, but chronic/severe infection can occur in neonates and in people with hypo- or agammaglobulinemia (Harrison 22e p.1168-1169).
pitfalls: Failing to recognize partially or incompletely treated bacterial meningitis, which can produce a lymphocytic-predominant CSF that mimics viral meningitis (p.1167)
Up to 15% of enteroviral meningitis patients (most often young infants) have a NORMAL CSF leukocyte count, so a normal cell count does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1168)

PMNs may predominate during the first 48 h of viral meningitis (e.g., echovirus 9, WNV, EEE, mumps); WNV PMN pleocytosis occurs in ~45% and can persist a week or more before shifting to lymphocytes — do not assume early neutrophilia means bacterial infection (p.1167-1168)
Treating a normal CSF glucose as ruling out viral meningitis is wrong, but conversely low CSF glucose can occur in 10-30% of mumps or LCMV and rarely with enteroviruses, HSV-2, or VZV (p.1167)
CSF viral culture has generally poor sensitivity for viral meningitis (unlike its utility in bacterial infection), so reliance on culture alone underdiagnoses (p.1167)
Enterovirus detected in stool is NOT diagnostic of acute CNS infection — it may reflect residual shedding from a prior infection or asymptomatic carriage during epidemics (p.1167)
Enteroviral RT-PCR has low sensitivity for EV71; specific testing may be required (p.1168)
EBV CSF PCR false-positives may reflect viral reactivation or latent viral DNA in recruited lymphocytes rather than true EBV meningitis (p.1168)
Routine serology is unhelpful for high-seroprevalence viruses (HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV) (p.1167)
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not give a formal severity grading for viral meningitis; it instead frames disposition by risk. Immunocompetent patients with a classic CSF profile (lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, negative Gram stain), no focal signs, and no significant alteration in consciousness may not require hospitalization if home monitoring and follow-up are assured. Hospitalization is indicated for immunocompromised patients, those with significant alteration in consciousness, seizures, or focal signs suggesting encephalitis/parenchymal involvement, and those with an atypical CSF profile (Harrison 22e p.1169).
